chapters.title: A Plug for Every Socket
chapters.tease: MCP is one standard interface between AI applications and the tools and data they need.

chapters.title: Multiplication Is the Enemy
chapters.tease: Point-to-point integrations multiply; a shared protocol turns N times M into N plus M.

chapters.title: Life Before the Protocol
chapters.tease: Function calling was the right primitive; the bespoke glue around it was the problem MCP solves.

chapters.title: A Short History of a Young Standard
chapters.tease: Open-sourced in November 2024, adopted through 2025, handed to the Linux Foundation that December.

chapters.title: The Model Only Talks
chapters.tease: The model never calls a tool; it asks in text, and the host decides whether the call happens.

chapters.title: Context Is the Product
chapters.tease: MCP exists to get the right context to the model on demand, and context always costs space.

chapters.title: Borrowed Ideas, Honestly Credited
chapters.tease: MCP borrows its shape from LSP and its envelope from JSON-RPC, and the borrowing is its strength.

chapters.title: What MCP Is Not
chapters.tease: MCP is not an agent framework, an API, a security model or a quality badge. It is a protocol.

chapters.title: The Shape of an Ecosystem
chapters.tease: Servers, hosts, SDKs and registries feed a two-way network effect, and a quality problem with it.

chapters.title: Your First Ten Minutes
chapters.tease: Connect one small, safe server, watch a real tool call, then verify the answer yourself.

chapters.title: Three Roles, One Conversation
chapters.tease: Host, client and server: nearly every MCP confusion comes from blurring two of the three roles.

chapters.title: The Host Holds the Keys
chapters.tease: Only the host sees the user, the whole conversation and every tool, so judgement belongs to it.

chapters.title: One Client per Server
chapters.tease: Each server gets its own client and session, isolated on the wire but sharing the model's context.

chapters.title: Servers Should Be Boring
chapters.tease: The best servers do one domain predictably with a modest set of well-described tools.

chapters.title: Local and Remote
chapters.tease: Where a server runs decides how it starts, authenticates, updates and what you should fear.

chapters.title: A Conversation With Memory
chapters.tease: An MCP connection is a session with a handshake, an operating phase and a shutdown, not a REST call.

chapters.title: Who Controls What
chapters.tease: Tools, resources and prompts differ by who decides to use them: model, application or user.

chapters.title: The Model Never Dials Out
chapters.tease: The model has no network, files or credentials; every request crosses points that can say no.

chapters.title: Many Servers, One Host
chapters.tease: The host composes many servers into one menu, which brings naming, overlap, volume and trust issues.

chapters.title: Gateways and Middlemen
chapters.tease: A gateway between host and servers adds control, but must relay both ways and carry identity.

chapters.title: Three Server Primitives
chapters.tease: Servers offer tools, resources and prompts: verbs, nouns and recipes. Almost everything fits one.

chapters.title: Tools Are Verbs
chapters.tease: A tool is a name, a description and a schema, all written for a reader who cannot see your code.

chapters.title: What Comes Back
chapters.tease: A tool result can carry content blocks, typed structured content and an error flag. Use all three.

chapters.title: Resources Are Nouns
chapters.tease: Resources are data addressed by URI, offered by the server and curated by the host.

chapters.title: Things That Change
chapters.tease: Notifications tell the other side that something changed; the client must fetch again to see what.

chapters.title: Prompts Are Recipes
chapters.tease: A prompt is a reusable, user-chosen template that carries the server author's expertise.

chapters.title: Sampling: The Server Asks the Model
chapters.tease: Sampling lets a server borrow the host's model, with a human able to review both ways.

chapters.title: Elicitation: The Server Asks the Human
chapters.tease: Elicitation lets a server ask the user a quick question mid-task, and never via a form for secrets.

chapters.title: Roots: Where You May Wander
chapters.tease: Roots tell a server which folders are in scope. They orient it, but they are advisory, not a fence.

chapters.title: The Small Print Utilities
chapters.tease: Progress, cancellation, logging, completion, ping and tasks separate solid servers from prototypes.

chapters.title: JSON-RPC in One Sitting
chapters.tease: Every MCP message is a JSON-RPC request, response or notification. Learn three shapes, read any trace.

chapters.title: The Handshake
chapters.tease: Initialize, result, initialized: three messages open every session before any real work starts.

chapters.title: Capability Negotiation
chapters.tease: You may only use what the other side said it supports; the overlap is the whole usable protocol.

chapters.title: Agreeing on a Version
chapters.tease: Versions are dates. The client proposes, the server accepts or counters, the client proceeds or leaves.

chapters.title: stdio: The Humble Pipe
chapters.tease: The host runs a local server as a child process; stdout is sacred and only carries protocol messages.

chapters.title: Streamable HTTP
chapters.tease: Remote servers use one endpoint: POST answers in plain JSON or a stream, GET opens a standing stream.

chapters.title: Sessions and Resumption
chapters.tease: Over HTTP a session ID ties requests together; streams can resume and replay what was missed.

chapters.title: The Server Speaks First
chapters.tease: MCP is two-way: servers send notifications and even requests, and partial hosts silently drop them.

chapters.title: Waiting Well
chapters.tease: Timeouts, progress and cancellation turn a frozen interface into a patient one: make slow things visible.

chapters.title: Endings, Graceful and Otherwise
chapters.tease: Sessions end through the transport; good software closes cleanly, reconnects calmly and uses accurate errors.

chapters.title: Start With the Job
chapters.tease: Don't mirror your API one endpoint per tool. Design tools around the jobs users actually ask for.

chapters.title: Picking an SDK
chapters.tease: Use an official SDK, start with its high-level API, and drop lower only where you must.

chapters.title: Hello, Server
chapters.tease: The smallest useful server: define, register one tool, connect stdio, run it in the Inspector.

chapters.title: Names for a Reader Who Guesses
chapters.tease: Tool names and descriptions are signs for a reader who guesses; make them specific and clear.

chapters.title: Schemas as Contracts
chapters.tease: A schema is a promise about what you accept: type it, constrain it, describe it, and validate it.

chapters.title: Errors the Model Can Use
chapters.tease: Protocol errors go to the client; tool errors go to the model, which can read why and try again.

chapters.title: Pagination and Big Answers
chapters.tease: Lists page with opaque cursors; tool results should narrow first, then limit, then link.

chapters.title: Return Less, Mean More
chapters.tease: Don't pass the upstream dump through. Return the few fields the question needs, in words, with ids.

chapters.title: Honest Hints
chapters.tease: Annotations hint how a tool behaves, so hosts can decide; believe them only as far as you trust the server.

chapters.title: Changing Without Breaking
chapters.tease: Add alongside, deprecate, then remove: additive changes are safe, renames and reshapes break things.

chapters.title: Where Servers Get Plugged In
chapters.tease: Hosts come in five families, each with its own house rules. Design for tools and treat the rest as extras.

chapters.title: Claude Code: Adding a Server
chapters.tease: One command adds a server to Claude Code; one more checks it. Skipping the check is how afternoons vanish.

chapters.title: Scopes and the Shared File
chapters.tease: Local, project or user scope decides who gets a server. The shared .mcp.json shares trust as well as tools.

chapters.title: Living With Many Tools
chapters.tease: A hundred and fifty tools need names, search, rules and limits, or the session drowns before work begins.

chapters.title: Mentions and Commands
chapters.tease: In Claude Code, resources become @-mentions and prompts become slash commands. Both are easy to miss.

chapters.title: Claude Desktop and Local Bundles
chapters.tease: Claude Desktop made local servers approachable: from a fragile JSON file to a one-click extension bundle.

chapters.title: Connectors on Claude
chapters.tease: On Claude web and mobile, servers are called connectors: remote servers you sign in to with your own account.

chapters.title: MCP Through the API
chapters.tease: From code: the API connector for a quick call, the Agent SDK for real agents. Either way, you are the host.

chapters.title: Other Hosts, Same Plug
chapters.tease: A server built once works in many hosts. The plug fits, the behaviour varies, so keep a compatibility matrix.

chapters.title: Claude Code as a Server
chapters.tease: Run claude mcp serve and Claude Code lends its file and shell tools to another host. Hands, not head.

chapters.title: Why stdio Skips the Question
chapters.tease: A local stdio server runs as you, so it skips authorisation. A remote server must earn trust every time.

chapters.title: OAuth in Plain Words
chapters.tease: Four roles and one flow: the user signs in at the auth server, and the client gets a limited, expiring token.

chapters.title: The Server Is a Resource Server
chapters.tease: An MCP server is an OAuth resource server. Issuing tokens is somebody else’s job; validating them is yours.

chapters.title: Discovery: Where Do I Log In
chapters.tease: From a bare URL, a chain of small metadata documents tells the host where to send you to sign in.

chapters.title: Who Is This Client
chapters.tease: Which client is asking? Pre-register it, register it dynamically, or let the client’s own URL vouch for it.

chapters.title: The Code Flow With PKCE
chapters.tease: The code flow with PKCE: a secret verifier proves that only the client that started sign-in can finish it.

chapters.title: Tokens With an Address
chapters.tease: A genuine token can still be meant for another server. Audience binding makes every token fit one door.

chapters.title: Never Pass the Token Through
chapters.tease: Forwarding the client’s token to a downstream API is forbidden. Every hop needs a token meant for that hop.

chapters.title: Scopes and Small Keys
chapters.tease: Design scopes around risk, ask for a small key first, and step up consent only when a door needs it.

chapters.title: Enterprise Identity
chapters.tease: In a company, MCP access should be granted, logged and revoked in one place: the identity provider.

chapters.title: Every Server Is a Stranger
chapters.tease: Every server is a stranger, and everything a stranger says is data, not instructions.

chapters.title: Injection Through the Side Door
chapters.tease: Planted text in a page, email or ticket can steer an agent. Nothing is hacked; the combination is the hole.

chapters.title: Poisoned Descriptions
chapters.tease: Tool descriptions are read in full by the model and skimmed by humans. Poison hides in the part nobody reads.

chapters.title: The Rug Pull
chapters.tease: You approved the server; three weeks later it changed. Approval is a snapshot, so pin versions and diff.

chapters.title: The Dangerous Triangle
chapters.tease: Private data, untrusted input and a way out: any two are a tool, all three are someone else’s opportunity.

chapters.title: The Confused Deputy
chapters.tease: A proxy with one static client ID lets an attacker reuse a user’s remembered consent. Ask per client.

chapters.title: Least Privilege, Practically
chapters.tease: Least privilege pays unusually well when the one holding the privileges is a model that can be talked round.

chapters.title: Shadowing and Look-Alikes
chapters.tease: All descriptions share the model’s context, so one server can whisper about another’s tools, or pose as it.

chapters.title: Local Servers Run as You
chapters.tease: A local server runs as you and can touch everything you can, unless you sandbox it or go remote.

chapters.title: Consent That Means Something
chapters.tease: Approval is the backstop for every attack, but only if prompts are rare, specific and worth reading.

chapters.title: The Inspector
chapters.tease: Before a model sees your server, see it yourself. The Inspector shows exactly what the model will read.

chapters.title: Testing Below the Model
chapters.tease: Most of a server can be tested without a model: unit tests, contract tests, and a few integration runs.

chapters.title: Testing With the Model
chapters.tease: Only a model can tell you whether models use your server well. Run tasks, read transcripts, fix the words.

chapters.title: Debugging the Pipe
chapters.tease: Most connection failures are the same few problems in different costumes. Check them in order.

chapters.title: Packaging Local Servers
chapters.tease: A server that only runs on its author’s laptop is a hobby. Package it, pin it, and test a clean install.

chapters.title: Going Remote
chapters.tease: Going remote turns a program into an operation: one HTTPS endpoint, stateless if possible, staged rollout.

chapters.title: Seeing What Happened
chapters.tease: When an agent misbehaves, ask what happened. Logs, traces and metrics per tool call are how you answer.

chapters.title: Rate Limits and Restraint
chapters.tease: Agents are diligent at machine speed. Limit calls, explain limits so a model can act, and design restraint in.

chapters.title: Registries and Discovery
chapters.tease: The official MCP Registry is a catalogue of who published what, not a store of code. Others curate on top.

chapters.title: A Server People Trust
chapters.tease: People let a server in when it sends small, checkable signals: docs, versions, provenance, security, support.

chapters.title: Shadow Servers
chapters.tease: People run more servers than anyone knows. Find them without blame, then make the approved path easier.

chapters.title: Allowlists and Managed Settings
chapters.tease: A denylist names yesterday’s problems; an allowlist decides about today. Managed settings make it stick.

chapters.title: Gateways as Policy Points
chapters.tease: A gateway between hosts and servers is where an organisation’s rules meet the protocol’s messages.

chapters.title: Audit Trails
chapters.tease: No single component knows what an agent did. Correlate host, identity, gateway and server logs by request ID.

chapters.title: Build, Buy or Borrow
chapters.tease: For any integration, ask in order: is there a vendor server, a good community one, or must you build small?

chapters.title: The Spec Moves
chapters.tease: The spec moves through public proposals and dated revisions. Build on the slow centre; watch the fast edges.

chapters.title: Agents Talking to Agents
chapters.tease: MCP connects models to tools. Agent protocols connect peers. If you can describe it as a tool, use MCP.

chapters.title: What Stays Hard
chapters.tease: The protocol made connection easy. Trust, identity across hops, discovery quality and context remain hard.

chapters.title: A Checklist for Strangers
chapters.tease: Vet the stranger, size the key, choose when to ask, and keep watching. That is most of it.

chapters.title: A Promise Between Strangers
chapters.tease: A protocol is a promise between strangers. MCP works when the promises are kept, and checked.
